analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student loan interest rates nearly in half and raises Pell Grants.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors in April 2006 and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut interest rates on federal student loans from 6.8% to 3.4% for students and from 8.5% to 4.25% for parents, starting July 2006. It would have raised the maximum Pell Grant—the main federal scholarship for low-income students—in steps from $4,500 to $6,000 by 2012, with yearly increases after that tied to inflation. It also would have let students combine their loans while still in school and ended a rule forcing borrowers to consolidate with their current lender.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers would pay roughly half the interest on new subsidized federal loans, and parents borrowing for their children's education would see rates drop from 8.5% to 4.25% [S2] [S3]. Low-income students would get larger Pell Grants, rising to a $6,000 maximum by 2012 and indexed to inflation thereafter [S2] [S3]. Borrowers could consolidate loans while still in school, easing the transition to repayment, and could shop for a consolidation deal with any lender instead of being locked to their current one [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the interest rate on new subsidized federal student loans from 6.8% to 3.4% and on parent loans from 8.5% to 4.25% under both the guaranteed and direct loan programs [S2] [S3].

Raises the maximum Pell Grant in steps to $6,000 by the 2011-2012 school year, with future increases tied to the Consumer Price Index, and makes the funding automatic rather than dependent on annual appropriations [S2] [S3].
Lets students consolidate their guaranteed federal loans while still enrolled, rather than waiting until they leave school [S2] [S3].
Repeals the single holder rule, which required borrowers seeking consolidation to go back to their existing lender, letting them shop among lenders instead [S2] [S3].

Caps administrative spending on the loan programs through 2012 and guarantees funding for the Direct Loan program's administrative account, replacing an authorization that was scheduled to lapse [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would cover the cost of the lower interest rates and the larger, automatically funded Pell Grants, which the bill appropriates as 'such sums as may be necessary' [S3]. Guaranteed student loan lenders would lose interest income on roughly half of each new loan and would lose the consolidation business the single holder rule steers to them; guaranty agencies would see their maintenance fees capped [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The rate cuts and the open-ended Pell appropriation are expensive: the bill commits 'such sums as may be necessary' every year without a funding ceiling, shifting costs onto the deficit [S3].

The benefit is not targeted by need: middle-income borrowers taking unsubsidized Stafford loans would have kept the 6.8% rate, while lower-rate subsidized loans would flow to all eligible borrowers regardless of income beyond the program's rules [S2].
Halving interest rates on all new loans subsidizes borrowers who could afford the current rate, which a critic would call a broad expenditure rather than focused aid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students and families, the benefits are large and concrete—lower rates on every new federal loan and a bigger, inflation-proof Pell Grant. The honest cost is real: the bill makes both programs automatic federal commitments with no dollar ceiling, and part of the rate subsidy goes to borrowers who did not need it. It is a broad, expensive affordability measure rather than a tightly targeted one, and its repeal of the single holder rule would come at the direct expense of the lenders the rule protected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate education committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 6, 2006 [S5] [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S5].
Durbin spoke about the bill again on the Senate floor on June 27, 2006, but the bill attracted no cosponsors [S5] [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Guaranteed student loan lenders kept the 6.8% rate on new loans and the single holder rule that steered consolidation business to them, and taxpayers avoided the bill's new spending—while borrowers and low-income students gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan lenders; borrowers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave floor remarks on it twice in 2006, and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over higher education law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 6, 2006 and took no action—no hearing, no markup, no report—before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no party split was ever recorded; the bill was a single Democrat's response to student aid cuts and never advanced in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have cut the interest rate on new loans roughly in half, cutting lender interest income, and repealed the single holder rule that forced consolidation borrowers to stay with their current lender. Keeping the status quo preserved lender revenue at borrowers' expense.
The bill capped account maintenance fees to guaranty agencies at 0.10% of outstanding loan principal, limiting a fee stream paid from federal loan funds.

The bill capped combined administrative spending for the guaranteed and direct loan programs through 2012 but also made the Direct Loan program's administrative funding automatic rather than subject to annual lapse, trading a ceiling for guaranteed money.
